advisor.summary: For an accrual-method business, the receivables aging is a standing inventory of income taxed when billed that may never be collected. Section 166 grants an ordinary deduction for business debts that became wholly worthless during the year and — for business debts only — for partially worthless debts to the extent actually charged off on the books. The review is an annual year-end sweep: identify the dead accounts, document why they died, book the charge-offs, and stop paying tax on phantom income. Cash-method businesses have nothing to deduct — the unpaid invoice was never income — so confirming the method is the first step, not a footnote. The model applies the charged-off amount as an ordinary entity deduction; establishing worthlessness and the bona fides of the debt is file work the engine cannot do.
mechanics: §166(a)(1) allows the deduction for a business debt that became wholly worthless within the year — a facts determination built on debtor insolvency or bankruptcy, disappearance, failed collection efforts, and the passage of time; no formal charge-off is required, though booking one is best practice.

Partial worthlessness is narrower: §166(a)(2) allows it only to the extent the debt is actually charged off on the books during the year — under Reg. §1.166-3 the charge-off entry is a statutory prerequisite, not bookkeeping hygiene.

The deduction cannot exceed basis in the debt (Reg. §1.166-1(e)): accrual receivables carry basis because the income was recognized, while a cash-method taxpayer's unpaid invoice carries none — this review belongs on accrual files only.

Worthlessness is proven with objective evidence — collection letters, agency referrals, judgments returned unsatisfied, bankruptcy notices — and Reg. §1.166-2(b) confirms no lawsuit is required where the facts show a suit would not collect.

Only specific identified charge-offs count: the reserve method was repealed for non-bank taxpayers in 1986, so a book allowance for doubtful accounts deducts nothing until individual accounts are written off.
A later recovery of a deducted debt is income in the recovery year under the tax-benefit rule — no amended return, just pickup when the surprise check arrives.

authority.note: The bad-debt deduction: wholly worthless debts, partially worthless business debts to the extent charged off, and short-term capital-loss treatment for individuals' nonbusiness debts.
The basis limitation that shuts out cash-method taxpayers — unpaid fees and rents are deductible only if previously included in income.
Evidence of worthlessness: all pertinent facts considered, bankruptcy as an indicator, and no duty to sue when suing would be futile.
Conditions partial worthlessness on an actual charge-off booked during the year.

authority.cite: Dixie Dairies Corp. v. Commissioner, 74 T.C. 476 (1980)
authority.note: The multi-factor debt-versus-equity framework applied when a related-party loan is attacked as a capital contribution — the threshold every owner or affiliate receivable must clear.

requirements: An accrual-method taxpayer with receivables previously taken into income (or genuine basis in loaned funds).
A bona fide debtor-creditor relationship — related-party balances need notes, stated interest, and a real expectation of repayment.
Worthlessness established in the deduction year, backed by a documented collection history.
For partial worthlessness: the charge-off entry booked before year end.
risks: Timing is the leading audit theory: the IRS argues the debt went worthless in an earlier (often closed) year, or is not worthless yet, and wins whenever the file lacks a dated worthlessness event — contemporaneous collection records are the defense.
Related-party loans are the second front: owner and affiliate balances get recharacterized as equity or gifts under the Dixie Dairies Corp. factors, turning an ordinary deduction into nothing.
Cash-method owners who read about bad-debt write-offs will ask for one — zero basis means zero deduction, and claiming it anyway is an exam flag the return signer owns.
Book reserves are not deductions; conflating the allowance for doubtful accounts with identified charge-offs overstates the deduction by the entire reserve.
Recoveries are taxable when received — set that expectation at write-off time, not at exam time.
stateNotes: Conformity: states starting from federal AGI or federal taxable income conform to §166 automatically — the write-off requires no separate state computation.

PTET interaction: the write-off is an ordinary entity deduction that already reduces the base on which a pass-through entity tax election is computed; the engine sequences PTET after it, so no additional state-side benefit should be layered on.

Missouri: conforms through its federal starting points (RSMo §143.121 for individuals, §143.431 for corporations) with no bad-debt addback; an entity electing under the Missouri SALT Parity Act (RSMo §143.436) simply computes on the post-write-off income.
reviewChecklist: Client's accounting method confirmed as accrual (or basis otherwise established) before modeling any amount.
Each written-off account carries a worthlessness file: collection attempts, correspondence, bankruptcy or judgment evidence, and the year the facts crystallized.
Partial write-offs are supported by charge-off entries actually booked before year end.
Related-party balances are tested against the debt-versus-equity factors and documented as bona fide loans.
The modeled amount ties to the charge-off entries, not a general reserve.

client.teaser: Stop paying tax on invoices that will never be paid.
client.headline: Get your tax back on money you will never collect
plainEnglish: If your books count income when you send an invoice, there is a hidden cost. You pay tax on every sale — even the ones that never get paid. A customer who folded or vanished leaves you taxed on money you never saw.

The tax law has a fix. When an invoice becomes truly uncollectible, you can write it off and deduct it. That takes back the income you reported but never received. The key is claiming it in the right year, with proof you tried to collect.

We make this a year-end routine. We sweep your unpaid invoices, flag the dead ones, document why, and record the write-offs before December 31. Your tax bill ends up matching the money you actually made.
client.analogy: Paying tax on a bounced paycheck would feel absurd. This is the process for getting that tax back.
benefits: Deducts income you reported but never collected
Cleans up your books at the same time
If a written-off customer pays later, you simply report it then — no penalty
steps: WE review your unpaid invoices near year end.
WE flag the accounts that are truly dead and document why.
YOU approve the write-offs so we can record them before December 31.
WE claim the deduction on the return and track any later recoveries.
clientCommitments: Save collection emails, letters, and notices — they are the proof
Approve write-offs before year end, not at tax time

annualMaintenance: Fourth-quarter receivables-aging review with worthlessness documentation
Charge-off entries booked before year end and reconciled to the return
Written-off accounts tracked for recovery income in later years
deliverables: Annual bad-debt review memo with a worthlessness file for each account
Charge-off journal entries and reconciliation schedule

suggest.reason: Accrual-method businesses often carry receivables that are already worthless and deductible.
